paper_title: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to each layer's activations, while absorbing the corresponding inverse transforms into its weights. Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve over round-to-nearest quantization, we introduce Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. Despite executing the activation transforms at inference time, MACaQ adds only 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. MACaQ reaches lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and already matches their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11 times less quantization time. We further apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, illustrating the generality of its layer-local design and show quantization of a 122B parameter model in 64 minutes, using only 32.5GB GPU RAM.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Perhaps the central idea in recent neural network quantization strategies is the change of basis. To compute the matrix product between an input and weight matrix, we may transform the input by matrix and apply the corresponding inverse transform to the weights, leaving the product unchanged. If is chosen wisely, the transformed inputs and weights can be substantially easier to quantize. Two types of transform are widely used to ease quantization. First, activations and weights may be rotated into different basis using an orthogonal matrix Mrot. The Hadamard transform is especially popular because it can be applied in O(N log N) operations and tends to produce approximately Gaussian-distributed outputs (4). Second, individual channels may be rescaled using diagonal matrix Mdiag (29, 18, 21), thereby suppressing outlying channels and balancing the quantization difficulty of activations and weights. One potential downside of such change of basis is that, although the weight-side transform can be absorbed into the weights at quantization time, the corresponding input transform ostensibly needs to be applied online. Prior work often avoids this cost by propagating the input Figure 1. Prior work propagates the activation-side change of basis (labeled P) outside the linear layer to avoid runtime overhead. This incurs an engineering and quantization-time overhead, where for each layer suitable absorption target must be found. MACaQ instead applies lightweight transform online, preserving complete layer locality at negligible (ca. 2%) run-time overhead for sufficiently large layers. transform through the network and absorbing it into preceding layers. This approach is widely used because it can eliminate the explicit runtime transform (1). However, it also introduces dependencies between layers: applying the transform to one linear layer may require modifying its normalization parameters, preceding projections, residual branches, or other connected operators. In this paper, we argue for tolerating the overhead introduced by online transforms because keeping them online 1 provides different benefit: simplicity through layer locality. MACaQ confines every transform and quantization decision to single linear layer. No neighboring layer is modified to compensate for its quantization, and no basis transform needs to be propagated through the network. Eliminating these inter-layer dependencies allows each linear layer to be calibrated, transformed, and quantized independently. This simplifies application to new architectures, enables layers to be loaded and quantized one at time, and leads to substantially faster quantization. Furthermore, all linear layers can benefit from online basis transforms, where in some architectures not all layers can have absorbed basis transforms. The cost of this design choice is small. MACaQ uses only per-channel scale and block-Hadamard transform online. Their cost grows with the input dimension, whereas the cost of the subsequent matrix multiplication also grows with the output dimension. Consequently, their relative overhead diminishes for larger layers. We measure an end-to-end decode overhead of 2.3% for Qwen3-32B in vLLM, while obtaining better qualityquantization-time trade-off than prior MXFP4 methods. Figure 2. Quantization time vs. WikiText-2 perplexity on Llama-3-8B (OCP MXFP4 W4A4), all measured on the same hardware. MACaQ is run with different number of flips and calibration tokens, the other methods where possible scale by calibration tokens. MACaQ matches the best quality of these strong baselines in 11 less time. The main contributions of this paper are:

sections.title: Method
sections.content: We propose MACaQ, strictly per-linear-layer pipeline for W4A4 MXFP4 quantization. MACaQ achieves higher output quality than state-of-the-art MXFP4 methods while requiring up to 11 less quantization time, see Fig. 2. We show that retaining lightweight basis transforms online incurs only small inference overhead while eliminating cross-layer dependencies. This simplifies engineering, see Fig. 1, enables layer-at-atime quantization with low memory requirements, and allows the same method to work on widely different model architectures. We introduce Flip-Refinement, fast Hessianaware coordinate-descent method that improves an initial round-to-nearest quantization assignment by moving individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. We provide efficient Triton kernels for MACaQquantized MXFP4 models in vLLM, achieving up to 3 end-to-end speedup over FP16 while limiting the overhead of online transforms to 2.3% on Qwen3-32B. Their cost is therefore independent of m, whereas the cost of the matrix multiplication grows linearly with m. For example, the smallest output dimension among the quantized linear layers of Llama-3-8B is = 1024, giving an arithmeticoperation ratio below 0.3%. This estimate describes arithmetic work rather than wallclock performance. The measured overhead also depends on kernel fusion, memory traffic, launch overhead, and the relative throughput of FP16 and MXFP4 operations. We therefore measure the actual kernel-level and endto-end overhead in later sections. Consistent with the analysis above, the relative overhead decreases with layer and model size. Quantization Procedure MACaQ preserves the layer-wise modularity of the underlying network: each linear layer has its own scaling factors, block rotation, Hessian, block exponents, and FP4 codes. Quantizing one linear layer never requires modifying neighboring normalization layer, projection, or residual branch. Forward hooks accumulate Hℓ = ℓ,kXℓ,k (19) for every linear layer ℓ over chunks of the calibration sequence. After collecting these statistics, each linear layer is independently scaled, rotated, exponent-screened, and refined. The original layer is then replaced by its packed MXFP4 implementation. Only the layer currently being processed needs to reside on the GPU (and for the calibration, outputs of parallel layers). The remaining model weights remain in host memory. This streaming procedure reduces peak device memory and allows the same quantization implementation to be reused across model architectures; all calibration and quantization logic is attached locally to linear layers. MACaQ offers two levers for trading quantization time against output quality: the number of calibration tokens and the maximum number of Flip-Refinement iterations. We produce the Pareto curve in Fig. 2 by sweeping these two parameters. Quality begins to plateau at approximately 2 106 calibration tokens and = 512 FlipRefinement iterations. For fair comparison we use = 128 and 2 105 calibration tokens for MACaQ in the experimental section (ca. 150s to quantize Llama3-8B). Besides this, our default configuration uses block size 32, exponent offsets {+1, 0, 1}, scale-balancing parameter α = 0.75, and ridge coefficient λ = 1.0. The parameters α and λ were chosen with wikitext train set validation run on Llama3-8B (sensitivity plot in appendix). The FlipRefinement implementation parallelizes across output rows and removes converged rows from the active set. We additionally compile the repeated refinement step with torch.compile; the initial compilation cost is amortized across layers with matching shapes.

sections.title: Experiments
sections.content: To show the effectiveness of MACaQ, we consider several different metrics. For comparison with literature baselines, we use model perplexity, as it is widely reported in quantization work and provides continuous and comparably reliable measure of model quality. We further report results on generative benchmarks. In generative settings, quantization errors may accumulate over generated sequences in ways that are not visible in fixed-text metrics such as perplexity, and these tasks are closer to many practical use cases. To illustrate the ease of generalization to new architectures, we also apply MACaQ to an image diffusion model. Finally, we measure the throughput of MACaQ relative to standard FP16 and other common baselines, both at the kernel level and end-to-end, and perform an ablation over the main components of MACaQ. The models we evaluate are drawn from the Llama-3 (11), Qwen3 (30), and Qwen3.5 (23) families. We evaluate perplexity on Llama models for comparability with prior work and use the reasoning-capable Qwen models for generative reasoning evaluations. For image diffusion, we use FLUX.2 Klein 4B (3), as it is openly available. Note that for MoE models we only quantize expert layers (also for baselines) otherwise we quantize all weights 5 quantize model that does not fit on the target GPU in its original precision into one that does. Generative Language Tasks Generative benchmarks are closer to many practical workloads and have the potential to reveal accumulation effects that may only appear when model generates sequence of tokens. They also avoid the limitations of multiple-choice QA evaluation highlighted by Dutta et al. (5). We evaluate MACaQ-quantized dense Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 MoE models on IFEval (31) and MATH-500 (13). MATH-500 contains free-form, non-multiple-choice mathematics problems that require reasoning chains to answer correctly. IFEval tests the instruction following capabilities of models in generation. Tab. 2 shows that MACaQ performs well on these tasks. Image Diffusion One of the key distinguishing features of MACaQ is that it can be applied to new architectures with minimal effort because it treats each linear layer in isolation. We demonstrate this by quantizing the linear layers of FLUX.2 Klein 4B (3) to MXFP4. This model also offers an official NVFP4 variant1, which provides strong baseline. NVFP4 uses microscaling groups of 16, rather than the 32 used by MXFP4, and requires approximately 4.5 rather than 4.25 bits per element. We find that MACaQ produces more faithful quantized model with respect to the original BF16 model when prompted with GenEval2 prompts (14). In Table 3, we report pairwise metrics ranging from signal-level similarity (PSNR), through perceptual similarity (LPIPS), to semantic similarity (DINOv3). MACaQ is closer to the original BF16 model across all these metrics. For qualitative illustration see Fig. 4. Kernel-Level Speed In Table 4, we compare the speed of single linear layer across different batch sizes and matrix dimensions. We compute XW using square weight matrices RNN, where {4096, 16384}, and inputs RBLN, where the batch size {1, 16} and context length 1for fair comparison we quantize the same layers that this official NVFP4 model quantizes with MACaQ Figure 3. Error bars show the standard error. and activations, but not the embeddings and lm-head (as is customary). All experiments are run on recent GPU with 504 TFLOPS (FP16), 96 GB memory and 1.79 TB/s memory bandwidth and use OCP MXFP4 format. Perplexity For perplexity measurements, we follow related work and calibrate on the WikiText-2 training set. We evaluate on the WikiText-2 (20) and C4 (24) test sets. WikiText-2 can therefore be understood as an in-distribution evaluation with respect to the calibration data, while C4 provides an out-of-distribution evaluation. We use context length of 2048. The results in Tab. 1 and Fig. 2 show that MACaQ matches or outperforms the baselines also in terms of quality, not only speed. Large-Model Quantization MACaQ can be used to efficiently quantize models that are too large to reside on the target GPU at full precision. To demonstrate this, we quantize Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on machine with single 96GB GPU. The model contains 122B total parameters, and its FP16 weights require ca. 244GB. MACaQ processes the model with lazy loading of layers and reaches GPU-memory usage of 32.5GB. Quantization takes 64 minutes (with 32 flips and 512K calibration tokens) and produces WikiText-2 perplexity of 5.14, compared with 5.06 for the full-precision model. sections.title: Related Work
sections.content: Hessian-Based Weight Compression Much of the current second-order quantization literature builds on OptiTable 5. Additive contribution of each MACaQ component on Llama-3-8B (MXFP4 W4A4), WikiText-2 perplexity at 512 Flips and 200000 calibration tokens. Configuration Wiki2 Full Precision (FP16) RTN + Hessian exponent search + micro-rotation + online second scale + flip refinement (= MACaQ) 6.14 8.28 8.09 7.65 7.08 6.87 0.19 0.44 0.57 0.21 mal Brain Damage (OBD) (15) and Optimal Brain Surgeon (OBS) (12) that introduced Hessian-based model compression. Optimal Brain Compression (OBC) (8) adapted this framework to layer-wise compression and introduced Optimal Brain Quantization (OBQ), using the layer-input Hessian = XX to minimize output reconstruction error. GPTQ (9) subsequently made this approach scalable to large language models by fixing the quantization order, allowing the same Hessian factorization to be reused across output rows. These methods assign weights sequentially and compensate the remaining unquantized weights. In contrast, MACaQ begins from cheap RTN assignment and then revisits the individual codes through incremental Hessian-aware updates. Coordinate-Descent Quantization QuantEase (2) and CDQuant (22) also formulate quantization (pure weightquantization) as coordinate descent and improve over one-shot assignments such as GPTQ by revisiting quantized weights. Our Flip-Refinement is designed primarily for speed in weight and activation quantization. It keeps each MXFP4 block exponent fixed and considers only the two E2M1 levels adjacent to the current code, allowing closed-form evaluation of the gain of each move. Basis Transforms Basis transforms have become central tool for reducing weight and activation quantization error. QuIP (4) popularized incoherence processing through Hadamard transforms for weight quantization, and QuaRot (1) extended Hadamard rotations to weightactivation quantization. SmoothQuant (29) used element-wise scaling to balance errors between activations and weights. Later work has optimized the rotation itself (19, 16), general per-layer affine maps, as in FlatQuant (28), or an element-wise scale, including weight-only quantization with AWQ (18) and calibrationfree weight quantization with SINQ (21) For microscaling formats, block-local rotations are often preferable to full-channel rotations, e.g. MR-GPTQ (6) and (27, 17), as they avoid spreading an outlier across multiple independently scaled quantization blocks. Other work has studied how these transforms interact: (7) analyze the sources of error in weightactivation quantization and recommend combining rotation and scaling, while (26) show that reducing concentrated activation mass makes Hadamard transforms more effective preconditioners.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: The core design decision of MACaQ, keeping everything layer-local, means that cross-layer error compensation is impossible. secondary pass with cross-layer statistics could be added on top, but would likely incur the slower quantization times of other methods. In our MoE experiments we restricted ourselves to expert quantization only due to practicality considerations. For the smallest model tested (0.6B parameters) the online basis transform overhead climbs to 8%, which starts to be relevant for some settings.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content: We have introduced MACaQ, fast and easy to apply MXFP4 quantization method for models based on linear layers. MACaQ matches or outperforms state of the art methods in quality and is faster. The key concepts that enable this are light-weight Flip-Refinement to replace GPTQ, novel Hessian-aware shared-scale optimization, and light-weight online basis transforms that enable the quantization processing to be local to each linear layer. All these features combined enable us to quantize 122B Qwen3.5 model in 64 minutes while using only 32.5GB GPU RAM.

OCP MXFP4 compliance The OCP MXFP4 specification requires the shared block scale to be power of two (E8M0). The DuQuant++ codebase provides both cast_to_eBm0() and cast_to_ eBm0_improved(), the latter permitting fractional-powerof-two scales, which are more expressive but not representable in the E8M0 scale field. We use compliant cast throughout, for all methods including our own, which accounts for small discrepancy with some of the numbers reported in the DuQuant++ paper. Rows are processed in parallel, while blocks are visited sequentially in random order using the updated gradients. We require relative improvement above 106 and recompute the gradients once per sweep to limit numerical drift. Refinement stops after at most eight sweeps or when sweep accepts no move. Per sweep over the n/4 blocks of an IQ3_S tensor, the match products amount to 2mnC operations in total, the length tables to O(nC), and the gradient updates to at most O(mn2) (if every row moved at every block; in practice far fewer), the same order as the once-persweep gradient refresh. The search thus scales linearly with the codebook size and never re-evaluates full row objective. For the down projection of Qwen3-4B (m = 2560, = 9728) with = 8192, the match products are 4.1 1011 operations per sweep. The inner dimension of these products is only four and the blocks are processed sequentially, so peak GPU throughput is not reached; eight sweeps of such tensor, including the sign and scale stages, take approximately 58 s. The FP32 score matrix is the only sizeable intermediate (84 MB at these dimensions); for larger tensors we process rows in chunks to keep it below 600 MB. All score products use FP32 with TF32 disabled, because the score differences between neighbouring candidates can be small. Self-tests 15 on real GGUF tensors check monotone sweeps, agreement with brute-force block minimization, and bit-exact repacking. Optional scale refinement. Exact block minimization thus does not guarantee better model perplexity: the searches can reach different local minima, and the layer objective is only proxy for model quality. Scale refinement further reduces the calibration objective but does not improve perplexity over codes-only refinement in the 4B comparisons. We therefore recommend codes-only block refinement for these formats. Setup. We quantize Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-14B with llama.cpp after applying MACaQs scaling and blockHadamard rotation. The corresponding activation transform runs online in patched llama.cpp. Hessians are estimated from 106 WikiText-2 training tokens, transformed into the quantization basis, and regularized with λ = 1. The output head uses the Hessian of the finalnormalization output. We compare the initial quantization, scalar flips restricted to legal on-grid moves with = 512, and eight sweeps of block refinement. Initial files are quantized either with or without llama.cpps importance matrix, computed from the same calibration text. Perplexity is measured with llama-perplexity on WikiText-2 and Pile sample; these measurements are not directly comparable to Tab. 1. Results. Block refinement is most effective without an importance matrix (Tab. 8). On Qwen3-4B in plain IQ3_S, it reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 13.06 to 11.81, compared with 12.31 for scalar flips and 11.83 for importancematrix initialization alone. On Qwen3-4B, block refinement reduces individual tensors Hessian objectives by 3042%, versus 1632% for scalar flips, and takes approximately 58 seconds per large tensor. With importance-matrix initialization, the gains depend on the format. Refinement changes IQ3_S perplexity only slightly, but improves IQ3_XXS on both models.
